title: The emotional influence of different geometries in virtual spaces: A neurocognitive examination
research_question: This paper aims to examine the connection between visual perception, human emotions, and architectural space, and to empirically measure and quantify emotional reactions to architectural space geometry.

participants.description: 112 individuals (45 male, 67 female), aged 21-46 years (mean age for males=27.82, SD=5.46; for females=26.54, SD=5.27). 12 were designers (mean age=33.8, SD=5.72) and 100 were non-designers (mean age=26.24, SD=4.73). 89 completed all physiological measurements.
participants.recruitment: Advertisements published on the web, in social media, and by word-of-mouth.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 27 virtual 3D architectural spaces, generated using Grasshopper and Rhino, with varying degrees of protrusion (P=0, P=4), curvature (C=0, C=4), scale (S=1, S=3), and proportional changes in height (H1, H1b, H2, H3) and width (W1, W1b, W2, W3). Participants experienced these in a VR environment (HTC Vive).

measures.instrument: X=Arousal score (derived from physiological measures) and Interest polarity (derived from human-centered operational measures)
Time in seconds spent in each virtual scene
EEG (Emotive Insight system, sensors AF3, AF4, T7, T8, Pz)

findings.antecedent: Participant group (Designers vs Non-Designers)
findings.mechanism: Designers may have a different sensitivity or processing style due to expertise.
findings.quote: On average, the designer (Ds) group had lower physiological measure results than those of the non-designer group (NDs).

findings.antecedent: Participant group (Designers vs Non-Designers) for protrusion, curvature, and scale MEVs
findings.test_statistic: F = 3.2590; df, 107 (protrusion), F = 3.2601; df, 107 (curvature), F = 3.9695; df, 107 (scale)
findings.mechanism: Designers may fixate longer due to their expertise in evaluating architectural features.
findings.quote: The D group obtained higher results than those of ND, only in their fixation duration (FD) measurements of measurable environmental variables (MEVs) of protrusion (F = 3.2590; df, 107; p < 0.0738), curvature (F = 3.2601; df, 107; p < 0.0738), and scale (F = 3.9695; df, 107; p < 0.0489; see Fig. 5).

findings.antecedent: Participant group (Designers vs Non-Designers) x MEV
findings.quote: There was no interaction effect between group and any MEV.

findings.antecedent: Protruded (P=4) and non-protruded (P=0) virtual spaces, moderated by participant group (Non-Designers vs Designers)
findings.mechanism: Non-designers show higher neural arousal/attention in response to protrusion, possibly due to less expertise in processing such forms.
findings.quote: both symmetric (protrusion (P) = 0) and non-symmetric (P = 4) showed a significantly higher ßratio among NDs, compared to Ds (F = 4.53413; df,85; p < 0.0361; see Fig. 6).

findings.antecedent: Curved (C=4) and sharp (C=0) virtual spaces, moderated by participant group (Non-Designers vs Designers)
findings.mechanism: Non-designers show higher neural arousal/attention in response to curvature, possibly due to less expertise in processing such forms.
findings.quote: Significantly higher ẞratio was also found among NDs in curved virtual spaces (VSs) (Curvature (C) = 4) and sharp spaces (C = 0), (F = 4.53796; df, 85; p < 0.0360)

findings.antecedent: Large (S=3) and small (S=1) virtual spaces, moderated by participant group (Non-Designers vs Designers)
findings.mechanism: Non-designers show higher neural arousal/attention in response to spatial scale, possibly due to less expertise in processing such forms.
findings.quote: in large spaces (scale (S) = 3) and small spaces (S = 1), (F = 6.07521; df, 85; p < 0.0157)

findings.antecedent: Different proportions of width (P(W)) or height (P(H)) of virtual spaces, moderated by participant group (Non-Designers vs Designers)
findings.mechanism: Non-designers show higher neural arousal/attention in response to spatial proportions, possibly due to less expertise in processing such forms.
findings.quote: and in the different proportions of width (P(W)) or height (P(H)) of VSs (F = 6.24984; df, 86; p < 0.0143).

findings.antecedent: Protruded (asymmetric, P=4) virtual spaces vs non-protruded (symmetrical, P=0) virtual spaces
findings.mechanism: Protrusion may increase arousal or cognitive load, reflected in pupillary dilation.
findings.quote: mean pupillary diameter (PD) was significantly higher in protruded (asymmetric) VSs (P = 4) than in non-protruded (symmetrical) VSs (P = 0), (F = 49.251; df, 325; p < 0.0001).

findings.antecedent: Sharp (C=0) virtual spaces vs curved (C=4) virtual spaces
findings.mechanism: Sharp forms may increase arousal or cognitive load, reflected in pupillary dilation, possibly due to higher prediction error.
findings.quote: PD was significantly higher in sharp VSs (C = 0) than in curved spaces (C = 4), (F = 273.823; df, 325; p < 0.0001)

findings.antecedent: Large (S=3) virtual spaces vs small (S=1) virtual spaces
findings.mechanism: Large spaces may increase arousal or cognitive engagement, reflected in pupillary dilation.
findings.quote: large VSs (S = 3) compared to small spaces (S = 1), (F = 96.903; df, 325; p < 0.0001)

findings.test_statistic: F = 103.171; df, 757 (overall proportions), t = -14.046 (low H1), t = 10.100 (narrow W1)

findings.quote: PD was significantly larger in low VSs (df, 757; t = -14.046; p < 0.0001), and in narrow VSs (df, 757; t = 10.100; p < 0.0001, see Fig. 7).

findings.mechanism: Sharp forms may increase peak arousal or cognitive load, reflected in maximal pupillary dilation, possibly due to higher prediction error.

findings.mechanism: Large spaces may increase peak arousal or cognitive engagement, reflected in maximal pupillary dilation.

findings.consequent: Maximal GSR amplitude (MGSR) and Rate of GSR peaks (GSRR)

findings.antecedent: Large (S=3) virtual spaces vs small (S=1) virtual spaces
findings.mechanism: Participants tend to stay longer in large spaces, possibly indicating higher preference or engagement.
findings.quote: participants from both groups stayed significantly longer in large VSs (S3 > S1; F = 6.3602; df, 325; p < 0.0121; see Fig. 10).

findings.antecedent: Participant group (Non-Designers vs Designers)
findings.consequent: Physiological measures (overall) for protrusion, curvature, scale, proportional height, and proportional width
findings.mechanism: Non-designers exhibit higher overall physiological responses to geometric variations, suggesting greater sensitivity or less habituation compared to designers.
findings.quote: a significant difference between the physiological measures of Ds and NDs, with higher values for NDs (P: F = 16.164515; df, 88; p < 0.0001, C: F = 16.247940; df, 88; p < 0.0001, S: F = 14.295772; df, 88, p < 0.0003, P(W) and P(H): F = 9.762352; df, 88, p < 0.0024).

findings.antecedent: Curvature (sharp C=0 vs curved C=4) in virtual spaces
findings.mechanism: Sharp spaces elicit the highest peak arousal, while curved spaces elicit the lowest, indicating differential emotional processing.
findings.quote: MPD was the highest of all of the selected physiological measures in sharp spaces (C = 0) and the lowest of all selected physiological measures in curved spaces (C = 4), (SE = 0.0723; df, 1625; t.ratio -6.444, p < 0.0001; see Fig. 11a and b).

findings.antecedent: Large (S=3) virtual spaces
findings.consequent: Pupillary diameter (PD) and GSR amplitude (high); Fixation duration (FD) and Beta Band Power Ratio (BBPR) (low)
findings.mechanism: Large spaces evoke a complex physiological response, with high arousal (PD, GSR) but lower sustained attention (FD, BBPR).
findings.quote: In large VSs (S = 3) PD and GSR amplitude were significantly high, FD and ẞratio were significantly low (sensorPz: SE = 0.0794; df, 1628; t.ratio -1.655; p < 0.0981; MPD: SE = 0.0753; df, 1628; t.ratio 3.867; p < 0.0001; FD: SE = 0.0756; df, 1628; t.ratio -3.330 0.0009; p < 0.0009; see Fig. 12a and b).

findings.antecedent: Small (S=1) virtual spaces
findings.consequent: Pupillary diameter (PD) (low); GSR amplitude, Fixation duration (FD), and Beta Band Power Ratio (BBPR) (high)
findings.mechanism: Small spaces evoke a complex physiological response, with lower arousal (PD) but higher sustained attention (FD, BBPR) and GSR.
findings.quote: In small VSs (S = 1), PD was significantly low, GSR amplitude, FD, and ẞratio were significantly high (sensorPz: SE = 0.0794; df, 1628; t.ratio -1.655; p < 0.0981; MPD: SE = 0.0753; df, 1628; t.ratio 3.867; p < 0.0001; FD: SE = 0.0756; df, 1628; t.ratio -3.330 0.0009; p < 0.0009; see Fig. 12a and b).

findings.antecedent: Narrow proportional virtual spaces
findings.mechanism: Narrow spaces may increase cognitive load or perceived threat, leading to longer fixations.
findings.quote: In narrow spaces, FD was significantly high compared to the other physiological measures (sensorA4: SE = 0.0770; df, 3344; t.ratio -3.135; p < 0.0094; MPD: SE = 0.0732; df, 3344; t.ratio 2.719; p < 0.0333; FD: SE = 0.0735; df, 3344; t.ratio 10.024; p < 0.0001; see Fig. 13a and b).

findings.quote: For example, for the scenes- H3, COPOS1H1, H1b, H2, C4P0S1, W1,W1b,W2 that were viewed less than 10 s, the model predicted an average satisfaction score of 2.1.

findings.antecedent: Specific VS geometries (COPOS2, C1P0S2, C3P4S2, C4P4S2, C4P2S2, C4P1S2, C4P0S2, W3) viewed for longer durations (4th to 27th)
findings.mechanism: Longer exposure to certain geometries leads to a moderate liking score, suggesting a more considered evaluation.
findings.quote: For the scenes COPOS2, C1P0S2, C3P4S2, C4P4S2, C4P2S2, C4P1S2, C4P0S2, W3 – that were viewed 4th to 27th, the model predicted an average satisfaction score of 3.5.

findings.antecedent: Specific VS geometries (C2P0S2, C3POS2, C1P4S2, C2P4S2, COP1S2, COP2S2, COP3S2, COP4S2, C4P3S2, COPOS3, C4P0S3) viewed for longer durations (4th to 27th)
findings.mechanism: Longer exposure to certain geometries leads to a moderate liking score, suggesting a more considered evaluation.
findings.quote: For the scenes- C2P0S2, C3POS2, C1P4S2, C2P4S2, COP1S2, COP2S2, COP3S2, COP4S2, C4P3S2, COPOS3, C4P0S3- that were viewed 4th to 27th, the model predicted an average satisfaction score of 3.8.

findings.antecedent: Curvature of space (more curved)
findings.mechanism: More curved shapes may reduce arousal or cognitive load, leading to smaller pupillary diameter.
findings.quote: the more curved the shape of space (in both symmetric and asymmetrical VSs), the smaller the pupillary diameter. This is manifested in the color gradient change (from yellow to blue) (Fig. 18a).

findings.antecedent: Protrusion of space (greater, in curved VSs)
findings.mechanism: Greater protrusion may increase arousal or cognitive load, leading to wider pupillary diameter.
findings.quote: The process of protrusion reveals the same effect, as the greater the protrusion of a space (in curved VSs), the wider the pupillary diameter. This reveals the color gradient as well (Fig. 18b).

mechanisms: Geometric properties of architectural space (protrusion, curvature, scale, proportion) influence visual perception and subsequent emotional states.
Expertise (designers vs non-designers) modulates physiological and behavioral responses to architectural geometry, with non-designers showing higher overall reactivity.
The 'peak shift effect' may explain positive interest in curved, large-scale spaces, where the process of recognizing these spaces is preferred.
Large spaces create a dramatic effect and a sense of awe, attracting prolonged engagement.
Simplicity and symmetry are associated with lower arousal and may promote relaxation, while complexity and asymmetry evoke more curiosity.
Narrow proportions and low heights can induce perceived threat or confinement, leading to increased arousal and negative interest.
Emotional dimensions are encoded in a gradient-like fashion, supporting a physiologically plausible mechanism for the coding of affective states (emotionotopy).
The necessity of using multiple sensors is important as it is impossible to attach a single measurement to a specific emotional state.
moderators: Exposure duration (short vs long viewing times)
implementation_implications: The findings can inform the design of affectively sympathetic spaces for various settings, including special needs children, educational structures, geriatric and rehabilitation spaces, and public/living spaces.
Designing large spaces can create dramatic effects and a sense of awe, suitable for large gatherings and prolonged engagement.
To create high excitement, extreme proportions or scale can be used.
Narrow spaces should be avoided if the goal is to prevent distressing experiences.

tables.description: Analysis of emotional response upon recognition of a VS, summarizing physiological measures, human-centered measurable variables, and geometrical space criteria, along with derived arousal scores and interest polarity.

limitations: Inability to precisely evaluate the relative contribution of individual measures to the total variance of emotional response.
The number of dominant measures (FD, BBPR) does not allow determining their actual contribution to the assessment.
Negative emotion appears easier to recognize, making it difficult to discern if the experimental setup was 'too negative' or if physiology was more 'engaged' in signaling negative emotions.
Negative experience is mainly connected to the absence of openings in VS, potentially associated with stress.
The study involved limited parametric changes in form.
The specific orientation of participants towards VSs might influence perceived threat (e.g., spikes with stronger protrusion).

environmental_features: virtual 3D rooms with curvilinear architectural features (rounded walls, ceilings, and furniture)
virtual 3D rooms with angular architectural features (sharp corners, straight lines, and angular furniture)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: approximately 2 seconds per stimulus presentation in an event-related fMRI design

theory_commitments.theory_name: Environmental Aesthetics / Preference for Curvilinear Forms
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Curvilinear forms are generally preferred over angular forms and elicit different emotional and neural responses, potentially due to associations with safety, nature, or processing fluency.
Investigates the neural underpinnings of aesthetic experiences, specifically how brain regions respond to different architectural geometries.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates the neural mechanisms by which architectural geometry influences emotional responses.

steps.to_construct: activation of brain regions associated with emotion and reward (e.g., anterior cingulate cortex, visual cortex)
